Milestone Description: Continuous Discovery is the practice of staying connected to the people a team is building for, instead of guessing what they need. Throughout a project the team keeps interviewing users, digging into problems, and testing its assumptions, and it turns what it hears into clear problem statements and a read on the competition. The name says it plainly: this is continuous. You learn a little at a time, all the way through, so the team is never designing in the dark.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: When teams stop listening, they start guessing, and guesses are expensive to build. Ongoing discovery helps the team rule out weak ideas early and lean into the strong ones, so the work stays pointed at problems that genuinely matter to the people using the product.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Discovery does not wait its turn and it never really ends. Teams run it while they are building and even after a launch, and they lean on it hardest whenever they hit a question only a user can answer. Like every milestone here, it is not a step in a line. It runs alongside the others and comes back around many times.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Requirements is the work of turning a rough idea into a shared picture of what to build. The team writes what it has learned as user stories and acceptance criteria, plain statements of what needs to happen and how everyone will know it is finished. In agile work you write just enough to get moving and keep refining as you learn, rather than trying to spell out every detail before anyone starts.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: Vague requirements are one of the most common places projects quietly go wrong. When the team shares a picture of what 'done' looks like, designers, developers, and clients stop working from different assumptions, and a lot of expensive rework simply never happens.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Requirements tend to sharpen right before a piece of work gets built, but they are never a one-time step. The team keeps rewriting them as it learns, so one part of a product can be in requirements while another is already being built and a third is being tested.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Scope is where a team decides what to take on now and what can wait. There are always more ideas than time, so the team chooses which pieces of work, the epics and features, to commit to and which to set aside for later. The goal is not to do everything, but to pick the right things to do first, and to keep adjusting that choice as the work teaches the team more.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: A project with no edges struggles to ship. Agreeing on scope keeps the team focused, sets honest expectations with clients, and protects everyone from the slow creep of 'just one more thing.'
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Scope gets attention early, but in agile work it is rarely set once and left alone. The team defines scope as it goes, shifting what is in and out as it learns, so scoping happens again and again, often while other parts of the product are being built or tested.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Implement is where the building happens and plans become real. Wireframes turn into working screens, and the product's components and brand come together. It is the hands-on, make-it-real work, and it usually takes the most time and energy, done in short repeating cycles rather than one long push.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: This is where the product's value actually gets made. Everything before it was preparation; this is the part users will see and touch, so the care the team puts in here shows up directly in the finished product.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Building does not wait for everything else to be figured out. One feature can be under construction while another is still being scoped and a third is already live. Expect implementation to run in parallel with almost every other milestone, in small cycles the team repeats as it learns.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Launch is the point where the work reaches real users. The team ties up the final details, plans how the release will roll out, and gets everything ready for the people who will use it. It is part careful checklist and part milestone worth celebrating, the payoff for the work that came before.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: A strong product nobody can get to helps no one. A clear launch plan means the work actually reaches people, so the team ships with confidence instead of uncertainty.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Launch is often pictured as the finish line, but products rarely launch just once. A team might release a small version early, then keep discovering, testing, and building well after. It helps to see a launch as one of many moments a product meets its users, not the end of the road.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Vision is where a team decides where it is headed and why the trip is worth taking. Before working through the details, the team steps back to describe the bigger picture: who it is serving, what success looks like, and a rough roadmap to get there. This becomes the reference point people line their work up against.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: Without a shared vision, teams drift and small decisions turn into debates. A clear vision gives people a standard to measure their choices against, which makes day-to-day decisions faster and more consistent.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Vision usually takes shape early, but it is worth returning to. As the team learns, the picture can change, so revisiting the vision partway through, even after a launch, is a healthy part of iterating rather than a sign that something went wrong.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Acceptance Testing is the team's reality check on whether the work truly does what it should. The team puts the work in front of users and against its own quality standards, and this is where problems like a confusing screen or a broken flow show up while they are still cheap to fix.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: Shipping something flawed costs far more than catching the flaw early, in both money and user trust. Testing against real people and clear criteria is how a team earns the confidence that the work is genuinely ready.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Testing naturally follows building, but it is not a single gate at the end. Teams often test one piece while building another, and it is common to run acceptance testing after a launch, checking how real use goes and feeding what they learn straight back into the work.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Milestone Description: Intake is the first real handshake of a project, where the team and the client get on the same page before the work begins. Together they sort out what the project is, what success means, and how they will work together, and they capture it in things like a statement of work and a set of shared agreements. It is short, but it sets the tone for everything after.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: Projects that start fuzzy tend to stay fuzzy. A good intake means the team is not guessing about goals or stepping on each other later, because the important questions got asked right at the start.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Intake usually opens a project or a new phase, but it can come back around. A new client, a fresh goal, or a big change can call for another intake partway through, so it is less a one-time start and more a reset the team returns to whenever the direction shifts.

Milestone Description: This is not a single stage but a catch-all for the work and habits that show up across the whole project. Some skills and ways of working are not tied to one moment; they run through everything a team does, from kickoff to launch. Think of it as the connective tissue of a project rather than a step along the way.
Why Is This Milestone Important?: It is a reminder that not everything fits neatly into a phase. Collaboration, learning, and steady improvement do not clock out after one milestone, and treating them as ongoing is part of what keeps a team healthy the whole way through.
When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: There is no single time for this one. It applies at every milestone, start to finish, and that fits how these milestones really work: not as steps in a line, but as pieces of work that run in parallel, repeat, and overlap as the team learns and adjusts.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile
